I, Algorithm

How online labor platforms manage workers
through algorithms, and how workers respond

A presentation on

Algorithmic Management of Work on Online Labor Platforms: When Matching Meets Control

Mareike Möhlmann, Lior Zalmanson, Ola Henfridsson, and Robert Wayne Gregory (2021)

Dan X-U

ISTM, UNSW Business School

30 September 2026

Who is the boss?

Which two statements are most likely to come from Uber drivers?

  1. The customer is my boss. Without customers, I have no business.

  2. Uber is my boss. It finds me customers.

  3. The algorithm is my boss. It tells me what to do and I cannot say no.

  4. I'm my own boss. I decide when to work and how much I want to work.

1

The case: Uber

Founded in 2009, Uber is a ride-hailing platform that connects riders and drivers through an app (Uber, 2026a).

  • ≈34,000 company employees worldwide at 31 December 2025 (Uber, 2026a).
  • Operations in over 70 countries and 15,000+ cities at year-end 2025 (Uber, 2026a).
  • 208 million monthly active consumers in Q2 2026, across rides and delivery (Uber, 2026b).
  • 3.9 billion rides and delivery orders completed in Q2 2026 (Uber, 2026b).
2

Theoretical motivations

1. Matching and control

Algorithmic management has two dimensions: (1) matching supply and demand and (2) controlling work. Upwork and MTurk emphasize matching; Uber combines both mechanisms (Möhlmann et al., 2021).

2. Platforms as organizations

A market perspective emphasizes transactions and work allocation. An organizational perspective examines how algorithms coordinate and control work (Möhlmann et al., 2021; Schildt, 2017).

Why Uber?

Extreme-case selection: Uber scores highly on matching and control, making it an informative case for theory development.

Research question

How does algorithmic management as implemented by the Uber app affect platform work?

3

Key concepts

Online labor
platforms (OLPs)

Digital intermediaries that connect workers with clients seeking services (Kuhn & Maleki, 2017).

Meta-organizations

Organizations that coordinate independent participants beyond their formal boundaries, without relying on conventional employment relationships (Gulati et al., 2012).

Uber example: Drivers participate in Uber’s platform, while Uber coordinates their work through algorithms and platform rules.

Algorithmic
management

Algorithms perform managerial functions, supported by organizational practices and systems (Lee et al., 2015).

Two dimensions in this study: (1) matching supply and demand; (2) controlling work (Möhlmann et al., 2021).

4

Research approach

Grounded theory

A method for developing theory through iterative data collection, coding, and comparison (Glaser, 1978; Charmaz, 2014).

  • Collect and analyze data together.
  • Compare accounts to develop categories.
  • Let emerging categories guide further data collection and theory development.

Question

If you were to conduct this study in the case of Uber, how would you use grounded theory to collect data, and what kind of data would you collect?

12

Who is the boss?

Self-employed
entrepreneurs

“I am my own boss.”

Full autonomy over when to work.
Determine their own workload.

Platform workers

“Yes, the algorithm
is my boss.”

Little autonomy over work direction.
Fully dependent on platform supervision.

Uber drivers

“The algorithm is my boss.
I am also my own boss.”

Freedom to decide when
and how much to work.

Algorithmic supervision, with little
room to negotiate or tailor the work.

Both states coexist.

13

The dual nature of platforms: Market and organization

Traditional taxi drivers

Illustrative unionized model

Collective voice: coordination, bargaining, and belonging through worker organization.

Protections: unions and applicable laws can support negotiations over pay and hours.

Uber drivers

Dispersed work, informal communities

Informal coalitions: isolated work and opaque algorithms prompt peer support and shared sensemaking.

Control: earnings incentives encourage long hours; sanctions enforce platform directives.

14

Summary and implications

Algorithmic management

Matching · Control

Work tensions

Execution · Compensation
Belonging

Platform responses

Uber is both a market and an organization platform.

Theoretical implication

Platforms combine market matching and organizational control, shaping work tensions and worker responses (Möhlmann et al., 2021).

Practical implication

Stronger legal protections are needed to safeguard drivers’ welfare, ensure fair pay and rest, and address algorithmic sanctions.

Critique & Reflection

Three waves could trace how algorithmic control evolves.

ID checks, removal of fare multipliers and Upfront Fares reshape monitoring and pay (Uber, 2016, 2021, 2022).

UK evidence links algorithm-driven dynamic pricing to lower driver pay and more waiting time (Binns et al., 2025).
